meta.what: English for each entry of Radak's Sefer HaShorashim the site shows. 'sense' is the line that stands in the root's row, so a reader scanning the list sees what the root means before opening anything. 'more' is what the open panel adds above his Hebrew: a few short labelled parts, each one thing his entry holds. Both are the guide's summary of his entry, not his words and not a translation, and the page says so.
rules: Report only what the entry holds. Where he names a view and its holder, name both. Where he disputes one, say so and say whom. Nothing from outside the entry.
Every Hebrew phrase quoted gets its English, or a reader without Hebrew gets nothing from the part that carries the point.
Lead with what the word means. Grammar is named only where he rests something on it, and then by what it does, since binyan names are not English.
Do not narrate the entry. 'He brings X for reading Y' is about the page; what X reads, and why, is about the word.
A part earns its place by being worth knowing. Where his entry is one line, the gloss is one line.
meta.keyed_by: Radak's headword as references/shorashim.json stores it, so an entry serving two roots (גרז for both גרז and גרזן) is glossed once.

אבד.sense: To be lost, or to perish; and where the verb takes an object, to destroy.

more.t: אֲבֵדָה, a lost object, the thing itself that is lost; אֲבַדּוֹן and אַבְדָן, destruction.

אֲרַמִּי אֹבֵד אָבִי (Devarim 26:5) he reads of Yaakov, not of Lavan: my father was a wandering Arami. Yaakov is the one lost, and he is called an Arami because he lived in Aram, twenty years there in great distress. The proof is Yaakov's own complaint to Lavan, by day the heat consumed me, and the frost by night (Bereishis 31:40).

צון.sense: The small livestock, the sheep and the goats.

more.t: Sometimes it takes in both together (Vayikra 3:6); sometimes one of them alone, as at Shmuel I 25:2, where it is the sheep, the goats being counted beside them; sometimes only the females (Bereishis 30:39); and sometimes the small livestock and the cattle together, as at Shmuel I 8:17, where the parsha names no cattle.
It is a collective and has no plural of its own, which is why the pesukim count with the singular: וּשְׁתֵּי צֹאן, two of the flock, and וְאַרְבַּע צֹאן, four of the flock.
Written with an alef and read as a vav, and it appears as צֹנֶה without the alef.

רמס.sense: To tread down hard and lay waste; and, spelled with a sin, to creep along the ground.

more.t: מִרְמָס, a thing trampled underfoot.

more.h: The word spelled with a sin
more.t: רמשׂ he says is close to it in sense, and the pesukim he brings are of what moves low along the ground: כָּל רֹמֵשׂ בָּאֲדָמָה, every creeping thing on the ground (Devarim 4:18), and הָרֹמֶשֶׂת עַל הָאָרֶץ, that creeps upon the earth (Bereishis 1:28), with the noun רֶמֶשׂ. He glosses them as treading and going.

גרז.sense: To be cut off; the גַּרְזֶן, the axe, is named from it, because it cuts the trees.

more.t: One line, on נִגְרַזְתִּי מִנֶּגֶד עֵינֶיךָ (Tehillim 31:23), I am cut off from before Your eyes.

אחה.sense: אָח, a brother, and אָחוֹת, a sister; and a second sense, אָחוּ, the marsh grass.

more.t: Almost all of the entry is the forms of אָח: אֲחִי in the construct, the plurals אַחִים and אַחְיוֹת, and which vowel the alef takes under each ending. In אָחוֹת, he notes, the vav stands in for the heh of the root.
At the end he gives the second sense, יִשְׂגֶּה אָחוּ בְלִי מָיִם (Iyov 8:11), can the marsh grass grow without water, where the vav again stands for that heh.

ענה.sense: To answer; and by further senses to bear witness, to raise the voice in song, and to afflict, whence עָנִי, the poor man, and עָנָו, the humble.

more.t: Mostly a reply, but sometimes it opens the speech, as וַיַּעַן אִיּוֹב (Iyov 3:2), where Iyov is answering nobody. In the passive, נַעֲנֶה and נַעֲנֵיתִי mean to be entreated, and he says he will return to that under the root עתר.
לֹא תַעֲנֶה בְרֵעֲךָ עֵד שָׁקֶר (Shemos 20:13), do not testify against your fellow as a false witness.
In song, וַתַּעַן לָהֶם מִרְיָם (Shemos 15:21), Miriam sang out to them; and in mourning, for which he brings Chazal's מְעַנּוֹת, the women who keen together, in Moed Katan.

more.h: Affliction, and what comes from it
more.t: וַיְעַנְּךָ וַיַּרְעִבֶךָ (Devarim 8:3), He afflicted you and let you hunger. To this belong עָנִי, the poor man, and לֶחֶם עֹנִי, the bread named for the affliction in Mitzrayim. Close to it he sets עָנָו and עֲנָוָה, lowliness of spirit, and so reads עָנִי וְרֹכֵב עַל חֲמוֹר (Zechariah 9:9), humble and riding on a donkey, with Targum Yonasan.

more.h: A matter one is busy with
more.t: עִנְיָן in Koheles, an affair or occupation. Here he brings his father, Rabbi Yonah and Rav Yitzchak ibn Giat; and he differs from Rabbi Yonah on אֶעֱנֶה אֶת הַשָּׁמַיִם (Hoshea 2:23), which he takes in the first sense, of speech.
מַעֲנָה, the line a plowman cuts across the field before turning back.

כבשֹ.sense: כֶּבֶשׂ, a lamb, with כַּבְשָׂה and כִּבְשָׂה for the ewe.

more.t: It is called a כבש while it is within its first year, because one older than a year is called אַיִל, a ram.

כבשׁ.sense: To subdue and to seize by force; also כֶּבֶשׁ, a ramp, and כִּבְשָׁן, a kiln.

more.t: וְכָבְשׁוּ אַבְנֵי קֶלַע (Zechariah 9:15) Rabbi Yonah reads as subduing their enemies with slingstones; Radak sets his own reading beside it, that the slingers themselves are overcome.

כֶּבֶשׁ is a ramp, and he takes it from Chazal in Zevachim: one sloping rise, not steps of stone or wood set one above another. That is why the mizbeach was given a kevesh, steps being forbidden by וְלֹא תַעֲלֶה בְמַעֲלֹת (Shemos 20:23), do not go up on My altar by steps.
כִּבְשָׁן, where stones are burnt for lime or earthenware is fired, as against the תַּנּוּר, in which bread is baked by sticking it to the wall.
כְּלִי חֶרֶשׂ (Vayikra 6:21), an earthen vessel, and יָבֵשׁ כַּחֶרֶשׂ כֹּחִי (Tehillim 22:15), my strength is dried up like a potsherd.

וַיִּקַּח לוֹ חֶרֶשׂ לְהִתְגָּרֵד בּוֹ (Iyov 2:8) he reads plainly: a potsherd to scratch himself with, the Satan having struck him with a dry boil. Others read חֶרֶשׂ as the name of the illness itself, which Iyov is said to have chosen out of all illnesses because scratching it gives some relief. Radak calls that reading far-fetched.

חרשׁ.sense: To be silent and to be deaf, with חֵרֵשׁ for a deaf man; and a second sense, to plow.

more.h: Why silence and deafness are one word
more.t: One who keeps quiet is as though he does not hear what is said, and makes himself deaf.

יַחֲרִישׁ בְּאַהֲבָתוֹ (Tzefaniah 3:17) he reads as Hashem keeping silent, out of love, over sins already done. רוּחַ קָדִים חֲרִישִׁית (Yonah 4:8) he takes as a wind so strong that men are made deaf by it, which is how Targum Yonasan renders it, שְׁתִיקָא.

נטה.sense: To turn aside or incline, and to lean toward someone.

more.t: כִּי יוֹאָב נָטָה אַחֲרֵי אֲדֹנִיָּה, Yoav had leaned after Adoniyah. Rabbi Yonah read אַבְשָׁלוֹם in that pasuk as standing for Shlomo; Radak holds that one man is never named in place of another, and says the same against him on זֶרַע יַעֲקוֹב וְדָוִד (Yirmiyahu 33:26). He brings the Ibn Ezra's reading beside his own.
מִטָּה, a bed, he writes under this root as well as under מטט.

מטט.sense: The root of מִטָּה, a bed; and of נָמוֹטּוּ, to be shaken.

more.h: Which root the word belongs to
more.t: Of בַּל נָמוֹטּוּ פְעָמָי (Tehillim 17:5), my steps have not slipped, he says that in the sefarim where the letter is doubled the word belongs here, and where it is not it belongs to מוט.

וַיֵּשֶׁב עַל הַמִּטָּה (Bereishis 48:2), מִטָּתוֹ שֶׁלִּשְׁלֹמֹה (Shir HaShirim 3:7) and מִטּוֹת זָהָב וָכֶסֶף (Esther 1:6), beds of gold and silver. He adds that they are written under נָטָה as well.
He weighs whether it belongs here too, and ends that it may be from נָטָה, where he has written it.

שֹבע.sense: To be sated and to have one's fill, and not of food alone.

more.t: לֹא תִשְׂבַּע עַיִן לִרְאוֹת (Koheles 1:8), the eye is never filled with seeing; שָׂבְעָה בְרָעוֹת נַפְשִׁי (Tehillim 88:4), my soul has had its fill of troubles; כִּי רַב שָׂבַעְנוּ בוּז (Tehillim 123:3), we have had our fill of contempt; and דָּוִיד זָקֵן וְשָׂבַע יָמִים (Divrei HaYamim I 23:1), old and full of days.
שָׂבְעָה and שֹׂבַע, fullness; הַשָּׂבָע, the years of plenty.

בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי (Shoftim 14:15), at Shimshon's feast, he holds is the Shabbos, and the fourth of the days of the feast rather than the seventh of them; שביעי, he says, never means רביעי, since a word is not found standing for its opposite. He brings the other reading as well, that it is the seventh day of the feast, and what follows from it.

דָּוִיד הַשְּׁבִעִי (Divrei HaYamim I 2:15) he holds against Rabbi Yonah likewise: the seventh is not the eighth. Shmuel I 16:10, which counts seven sons passing before Shmuel besides David, he settles by saying Yishai may have had a son from another wife, the brothers from David's own mother being seven with him.
שִׁבְעָתַיִם, seven times over.

ספר.sense: To count; in the intensive, to recount or tell; and the written word, סֵפֶר a book and סוֹפֵר a scribe. Separately, סַפִּיר, a precious stone.

more.t: סָפַר אֶת הָעָם (Shmuel II 24:10), he counted the people, and וְסָפַרְתָּ לְךָ (Vayikra 25:8), you shall count for yourself. The nouns are מִסְפַּר, a number, and הַסְּפָר, the count itself.
In the intensive it is to recount: סַפְּרוּ נָא לִי (Bereishis 40:8), tell it to me. He notes that he has set out the difference between telling and relating, ספור and הגדה, under the root נגד.

סֵפֶר, a book or a written document, and סוֹפֵר, a scribe, as בָּרוּךְ בֶּן נֵרִיָּהוּ הַסֹּפֵר (Yirmiyahu 36:32). לֹא יָדַעְתִּי סֵפֶר (Yeshayahu 29:12) he glosses: I do not know how to read it. The two senses lie close, he says, because writing a book is itself the telling of the matter.

מִי יְסַפֵּר שְׁחָקִים בְּחָכְמָה (Iyov 38:37) is read three ways, and he does not choose. Some take it from this root in the sense of counting. Rabbi Yonah takes it from writing. His father takes it from סַפִּיר, that He made them like sapphire, as in וְתַחַת רַגְלָיו כְּמַעֲשֵׂה לִבְנַת הַסַּפִּיר (Shemos 24:10).

Here too he brings the views and leaves them standing. Some say the precious stone of that name, and he notes that in סַפִּיר גִּזְרָתָם (Eichah 4:7) the comparison is one of worth and greatness, not of colour. The Ibn Ezra says it is a red stone. The Gaon says it is white, the one called crystal. And the Midrash in Eichah Rabbah tells of a man who went to sell a sapphire in Rome: the buyer set it on an anvil and struck it with a hammer, and the anvil split and the hammer broke while the stone stood where it was. By that midrash, he says, it is the diamond, white and clear.

חלל.sense: One slain, חָלָל; to begin; to profane, whence חֹל, the ordinary; the flute חָלִיל and the dance מָחוֹל; and חַלּוֹן, a window.

more.t: וַיִּפְּלוּ חֲלָלִים (Shmuel I 31:1), they fell slain, and חַלְלֵי חֶרֶב מֵחַלְלֵי רָעָב (Eichah 4:9), better the slain of the sword than the slain of hunger. In the intensive the verb is to kill, and he glosses מְחֻלְלֵי חֶרֶב (Yechezkel 32:26) as those killed by the sword.

וַיָּחֶל נֹחַ (Bereishis 9:20), Noach began, and הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה אָחֵל תֵּת פַּחְדְּךָ (Devarim 2:25), this day I begin to put your dread. The noun is תְּחִלָּה, as תְּחִלַּת חָכְמָה יִרְאַת י"י (Mishlei 9:10).

כִּי חִלֵּל יְהוּדָה (Malachi 2:11), Yehudah has profaned. On אֲשֶׁר נָטַע כֶּרֶם וְלֹא חִלְּלוֹ (Devarim 20:6) he explains that he has not made it chol, since it is holy until he redeems it. From this comes חֹל, the ordinary, set against קֹדֶשׁ, and לֹא יַחֵל דְּבָרוֹ (Bamidbar 30:3), which he reads as not making his word chol but letting it stand, as if he had declared it holy. חָלִילָה, far be it, he counts here too, profaning standing in place of holiness.

מְחַלְּלִים בַּחֲלִלִים (Melachim I 1:40), piping upon flutes. The instrument is the חָלִיל, and he says it is named for being hollow; Rashi gives its name in the vernacular, and Yonasan renders it צֶלְצְלִין. From the same he takes מָחוֹל, the dance, named because they play flutes within it.
וּבִמְחִלּוֹת עָפָר (Yeshayahu 2:19), hollows dug under the earth after the manner of caves; and חַלּוֹן, a window, as חַלּוֹן הַתֵּבָה (Bereishis 8:6).

דבר.sense: To speak, with דָּבָר for a word, a matter, or a thing; and separately דֶּבֶר, plague, מִדְבָּר, wilderness, דְּבוֹרָה, a bee, and דְּבִיר, the inner chamber.

more.t: The long part of the entry. Saying, אמירה, is never without someone spoken to, whether or not the pasuk says who: אִמְרִי נָא אֲחֹתִי אָתְּ (Bereishis 12:13) means say it to those who ask you. Speaking, דבור, points at speech itself, the thing that belongs to man, which is why one says a man is living and speaking and not living and saying. And speaking is not used of what cannot speak, even by way of figure, where telling is: וְיֹאמְרוּ לְךָ הִנֵּנוּ (Iyov 38:35) and וִיסַפְּרוּ לְךָ דְּגֵי הַיָּם (Iyov 12:8). The two take different words after them as well: saying takes אֶל and the lamed alone, while speaking takes בְּ and אֶת besides.

more.h: A matter, or anything at all
more.t: עַל דְּבַר הַכֶּסֶף (Bereishis 43:18), on the matter of the money; אֵין מַחְסוֹר כָּל דָּבָר (Shoftim 19:19), no lack of anything in the world; and where a word means thought rather than speech, אָמַרְתִּי אֲנִי בְּלִבִּי (Koheles 2:1), I said in my heart, which he glosses as I thought.
דֶּבֶר כָּבֵד מְאֹד (Shemos 9:3), a very heavy pestilence, which he calls a sense of death, and from it אֱהִי דְבָרֶיךָ מָוֶת (Hoshea 13:14).

כְּעֵדֶר בְּתוֹךְ הַדָּבְרוֹ he takes as its driving or its custom. The right account, he says, is that מִדְבָּר is named from this: the place of pasture where the shepherd drives his flock, as וַיִּנְהַג אֶת הַצֹּאן אַחַר הַמִּדְבָּר (Shemos 3:1). From the same he takes דֹּבְרוֹת, rafts, the great logs tied at their heads and driven along the sea.

more.h: The bee and the inner chamber
more.t: דְּבוֹרָה, a bee, as עֲדַת דְּבוֹרִים (Shoftim 14:8); and דְּבִיר, the inner house where the Aron was set, the outer one being called the הֵיכָל.

עבר.sense: To pass or cross over; and by further senses to surpass, to be angry, עֵבֶר a side, עִבְרִי a Hebrew, and בַּעֲבוּר, because of.

more.t: לְעָבְרְךָ בִּבְרִית (Devarim 29:11), for you to pass into a covenant, which he explains from the practice itself: the animal is cut in two and the parties to the covenant pass between the pieces, as אֲשֶׁר עָבַר בֵּין הַגְּזָרִים הָאֵלֶּה (Bereishis 15:17). לַעֲבֹר בְּרִיתוֹ (Devarim 17:2) is the opposite, to forsake the covenant and transgress it, as though it said מעל בריתו.

מַעֲבַר יַבֹּק (Bereishis 32:23), the ford of Yabok, and עָבְרוּ מַעְבָּרָה (Yeshayahu 10:29). Where the verb takes an object it is to bring across or to pass through: הֶעֱבִיר אֶת בְּנוֹ בָּאֵשׁ (Melachim II 21:6).

עֹבֵר לַסֹּחֵר (Bereishis 23:16), current with the merchant. The silver, he says, is sometimes taken in by the merchant and sometimes paid out by him, so that it is always passing to and from his hand.
וַיַּעֲבֹר אֶת הַכּוּשִׁי (Shmuel II 18:23), he outran the Kushi; and so עָבְרוּ דִבְרֵי רָע (Yirmiyahu 5:28), they did worse than other wicked men had done.
מֵעֵבֶר הַנָּהָר (Shmuel II 10:16), from the side of the river, and מִכָּל עֲבָרָיו (Melachim I 5:4), from all its sides. עִבְרִי אָנֹכִי (Yonah 1:9) he takes as being of the family of Ever.

עֹבֵר מִתְעַבֵּר עַל רִיב לֹּא לוֹ (Mishlei 26:17), one who passes by and grows angry at a quarrel not his own, and וַיִּתְעַבֵּר, as at Devarim 3:26. The noun is עֶבְרָה, as עֶבְרָה וָזַעַם וְצָרָה (Tehillim 78:49): wrath and burning anger.

מֵעֲבוּר הָאָרֶץ (Yehoshua 5:11), the grain of the land; he suggests that the grain of the year past may be called עבור while that of the year coming is תבואה. And בַּעֲבוּר is because of, as בַּעֲבוּר דָּוִד (Tehillim 132:10), for David's sake. He remarks that the word is not rightly used without its bet, as some of the paytanim use it.

פנה.sense: To turn and to face; whence פִּנָּה, a corner, and פָּנִים, the face. Where the verb takes an object, to clear away.

more.t: כִּי פָנָה אֶל אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים (Devarim 31:18), he turned to other gods, and פְּנוּ לָכֶם צָפֹנָה (Devarim 2:3), turn yourselves northward. לִפְנוֹת עָרֶב (Bereishis 24:63) he glosses as when the evening turns and comes on.
A corner is called פִּנָּה, a turning, because it looks upon the wall and its beauty; and from the same, he says, the face is called פָּנִים, because it turns this way and that.

לִפְנֵי, before; מִפְּנֵי, from before; and מִלִּפְנֵי, where both stand together. He asks how the mem, which shows distance, and the lamed, which shows nearness, can be joined in one word, since they are opposites, and answers that it means from the place that is before Hashem, which is the place where prophecy is received.

עַל פְּנֵי he often reads as during a life: וַיָּמָת הָרָן עַל פְּנֵי תֶּרַח אָבִיו (Bereishis 11:28), Haran died in the lifetime of Terach his father, and so עַל פְּנֵי אַהֲרֹן אֲבִיהֶם (Bamidbar 3:4). He reads לֹא יִהְיֶה לְךָ אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים עַל פָּנָי (Shemos 20:3) the same way, while I endure, which is for ever, and offers beside it that על פני there means to anger Me.
Where the verb takes an object it is to clear: וְאָנֹכִי פִּנִּיתִי הַבַּיִת (Bereishis 24:31), I have cleared the house, and פַּנּוּ דֶּרֶךְ (Yeshayahu 40:3), clear a way.

חרב.sense: To be dry, and to lie waste; חֶרֶב, anything that cuts, from a sword to a razor or a chisel; and חָרְבָּה, a ruin.

more.t: חָרְבוּ פְּנֵי הָאֲדָמָה (Bereishis 8:13), the face of the ground was dry, and וְנָהָר יֶחֱרַב וְיָבֵשׁ (Yeshayahu 19:5). The nouns are חָרָבָה, dry land, and חֹרֶב, drought and heat; the adjective is פַּת חֲרֵבָה (Mishlei 17:1), a dry crust. All of them together, he says, are dryness, drying and heat.

Here he is explicit: whatever cuts is called a חֶרֶב, whether of iron or a sharpened stone, as חַרְבוֹת צֻרִים (Yehoshua 5:2), knives of flint. It is a general name that is sometimes particular to the sword, and it takes in a razor, קַח לְךָ חֶרֶב חַדָּה תַּעַר הַגַּלָּבִים (Yechezkel 5:1); the chisel that dresses stones, כִּי חַרְבְּךָ הֵנַפְתָּ עָלֶיהָ (Shemos 20:22); and the tool that throws towers down, וּמִגְדְּלֹתַיִךְ יִתֹּץ בְּחַרְבוֹתָיו (Yechezkel 26:9).
וְהָעִיר הַזֹּאת תֶּחֱרַב (Yirmiyahu 26:9), this city shall be laid waste, with חָרְבָּה for a ruin and הֶחֳרָבוֹת for ruins.

On וְשַׂעֲרוּ חָרְבוּ מְאֹד (Yirmiyahu 2:12) Rabbi Yonah reports that some read this חָרְבוּ as the one in חָרְבוּ פְּנֵי הָאֲדָמָה and took it for a command; he turned them back from the Mesorah, which marks this חָרְבוּ as standing alone.

נצב.sense: Something set up: נְצִיב, a pillar of salt or a governor, and הַנִּצָּב, the haft of a knife.

more.t: נְצִיב מֶלַח (Bereishis 19:26) he glosses as a mound of salt. The stone set up to be served is a מַצֵּבָה; and the man set over a people is a נְצִיב, as נְצִיב פְּלִשְׁתִּים (Shmuel I 13:3) and שְׁנֵים עָשָׂר נִצָּבִים (Melachim I 4:7), officers set over the people.

וּמֶלֶךְ אֵין בֶּאֱדוֹם נִצָּב מֶלֶךְ (Melachim I 22:48): in Yehoshafat's day Edom had no king of its own, and the governor whom the kings of David's house set over them served them as king. He ties it to Yehoshafat walking in the way of Hashem, and notes that under his son Yehoram, who did evil, Edom rebelled at once and set a king over itself.

הַנִּצָּבָה לֹא יְכַלְכֵּל (Zechariah 11:16), the sick ewe standing in her place and unable to stir; and הַנִּצָּב (Shoftim 3:22), the haft of the knife, which holds the blade so that there is a handle to cut with.
He ends by saying that most of what he has written here may belong to the root יצב, where he has written their like, and that there is nothing to decide between them.

חיה.sense: To live, and to stay alive; whence חַיָּה for a wild animal, for the soul, and for a company of men; and חַי, alive, or of meat, raw.

more.t: וְחָיְתָה נַפְשִׁי בִּגְלָלֵךְ (Bereishis 12:13), that my soul may live on your account. It is also recovering from illness: עַד חֲיוֹתָם (Yehoshua 5:8), until they were healed, and וְיִמְרְחוּ עַל הַשְּׁחִין וְיֶחִי (Yeshayahu 38:21). Where the verb takes an object it is to keep alive or to let live, as מְכַשֵּׁפָה לֹא תְחַיֶּה (Shemos 22:17).

more.h: The wild animal and the tame
more.t: On זֹאת הַחַיָּה אֲשֶׁר תֹּאכְלוּ (Vayikra 11:2) he says the behemah is taken in under chayah. But אֲשֶׁר יָצוּד צֵיד חַיָּה אוֹ עוֹף (Vayikra 17:13) is of the chayah alone and not the behemah, since the behemah has no covering of its blood.

more.h: The soul, and the name Chavah
more.t: The neshamah is called חַיָּה, he says, because it lives for ever and is not as the body is; and the animal soul is called חַיָּה too, as וְזִהֲמַתּוּ חַיָּתוֹ לָחֶם (Iyov 33:20). חַוָּה is from the same, אֵם כָּל חָי (Bereishis 3:20), the yud turned to a vav so that the name should not be confused with the חַיָּה one eats.

more.h: Raw, and this time next year
more.t: Of meat חַי is raw: וְלֹא יִקַּח מִמְּךָ בָּשָׂר מְבֻשָּׁל כִּי אִם חָי (Shmuel I 2:15). כָּעֵת חַיָּה (Bereishis 18:14) he reads as this same time in the coming year, when it will be living. Since Chazal call a midwife חַיָּה he offers a second reading, that it means at this time you will be bearing a child; and by that usage he reads כִּי חָיוֹת הֵנָּה (Shemos 1:19) as saying the Hebrew women are midwives themselves and need no others.

more.h: A company, and a cluster of houses
more.t: חַיָּתְךָ יָשְׁבוּ בָהּ (Tehillim 68:11) and וְחַיַּת פְּלִשְׁתִּים (Shmuel II 23:13) are a company of men, and חַיַּת קָנֶה he explains as the company that carries reeds, meaning spears. Houses standing together that cannot be built up as a walled city are called a חַיָּה as well, and so חַוֹּת יָאִיר (Bamidbar 32:41). Rabbi Yonah says Arabic calls such a cluster by the same word.

שׁלח.sense: To send; to let loose or set free; to stretch out the hand; and the nouns שֶׁלַח, a weapon, and שֻׁלְחָן, a table.

more.t: שָׁלַח לִפְנֵיהֶם אִישׁ (Tehillim 105:17), He sent a man before them. His father reads יָדָהּ לַיָּתֵד תִּשְׁלַחְנָה (Shoftim 5:26) not as stretching out but as sending: Yael's hands were sent for the peg and for the workman's hammer, and the sending is ascribed to the hands because the hands are the chief part of the deed.

Close to sending is the loosing of a thing with nothing to hold it back. מְשַׁלְּחֵי רֶגֶל הַשּׁוֹר וְהַחֲמוֹר (Yeshayahu 32:20): out of the abundance of grain they turn the ox and the donkey loose to graze in the fields and do not mind it. נָוֶה מְשֻׁלָּח (Yeshayahu 27:10) stands open for whoever would bring his beasts in, and וְנַעַר מְשֻׁלָּח מֵבִישׁ אִמּוֹ (Mishlei 29:15) is a boy left free to follow his own desire.
שָׁלַח יָדָיו בִּשְׁלֹמָיו (Tehillim 55:21) and וְיָד אַל תִּשְׁלְחוּ בוֹ (Bereishis 37:22), with the nouns מִשְׁלוֹחַ יָדָם (Yeshayahu 11:14) and בְּכֹל מִשְׁלַח יֶדְכֶם (Devarim 12:7).

שְׁלֻחוֹתֶיהָ נִטְּשׁוּ (Yeshayahu 16:8), the spreading of boughs and branches; and from it an orchard is named, שְׁלָחַיִךְ פַּרְדֵּס רִמּוֹנִים (Shir HaShirim 4:13). The stream by Yerushalayim may carry the name for the same reason, מֵי הַשִּׁלֹחַ (Yeshayahu 8:6), because it spreads out among the gardens to water them.

more.h: Driving out, the weapon, the table
more.t: To drive away: וַיְשַׁלְּחֵהוּ, He sent him out מִגַּן עֵדֶן (Bereishis 3:23), and אֶל מִחוּץ לַמַּחֲנֶה תְּשַׁלְּחוּם (Bamidbar 5:3). שֶׁלַח is a weapon, וַיַּעַשׂ שֶׁלַח לָרֹב וּמָגִנִּים (Divrei HaYamim II 32:5). And the שֻׁלְחָן, the table, he takes from this root.

חבל.sense: Six senses: to take a pledge; to act corruptly and destroy; birth pangs; a rope, and so a measured district; stratagems; and a company of men.

more.t: לֹא יַחֲבֹל רֵחַיִם וָרָכֶב (Devarim 24:6), he shall not take a mill or an upper millstone in pledge. Most of the uses are the taking of a pledge, some the giving of one. יַחְבְּלוּ שׁוֹר אַלְמָנָה (Iyov 24:3) he reads as taking a widow's ox for a debt owed them, a thing forbidden because of her helplessness, or else as seizing it where no debt is owed at all, as כִּי תַחְבֹּל אַחֶיךָ חִנָּם (Iyov 22:6).

חָבַלְנוּ לָךְ (Nechemiah 1:7), we have dealt corruptly toward You; and where the verb takes an object, מְחַבְּלִים כְּרָמִים (Shir HaShirim 2:15), spoiling the vineyards, and לְחַבֵּל כָּל הָאָרֶץ (Yeshayahu 13:5).
חֶבְלֵי יוֹלֵדָה (Hoshea 13:13), the pangs of a woman in labour, and צִירִים וַחֲבָלִים יֹאחֵזוּ (Yeshayahu 13:8). All of them together, he says, are pangs and pains.

more.h: A rope, and a measured district
more.t: וַתּוֹרִדֵם בַּחֶבֶל (Yehoshua 2:15), she let them down by a rope. Because an inheritance is measured out with a rope, as וְאַדְמָתְךָ בַּחֶבֶל תְּחֻלָּק (Amos 7:17), a region is itself called a חֶבֶל: כָּל חֶבֶל אַרְגֹּב (Devarim 3:4). רַב הַחֹבֵל (Yonah 1:6) is the chief man of the ship, set over her ropes to work her as she should go.

more.h: What a man lies on at sea
more.t: On וּכְשֹׁכֵב בְּרֹאשׁ חִבֵּל (Mishlei 23:34) Rabbi Yonah says it is a thing made of ropes that floats on the water to mark where ships may anchor, so that a man lying on it is in danger; or else it is the chief of the ship himself, who lies at the head of the ropes and must watch them in great anxiety. Others say חִבֵּל is the mast, from which all the ropes hang. And the Gaon, Rav Saadiah, says the ship herself is called חבל, since she is worked by drawing the ropes and letting them go.

כִּי בְתַחְבֻּלוֹת תַּעֲשֶׂה לְּךָ מִלְחָמָה (Mishlei 24:6), which he glosses as the counsels and thoughts a man turns over in his heart to choose the straight one. And חֶבֶל נְבִיאִים (Shmuel I 10:5) is a company or a gathering. He suggests the two may be one thing, since thoughts are themselves a gathering of matters in the heart.

צפן.sense: To hide, and to store away; and צָפוֹן, the north.

more.t: אֲשֶׁר צָפַנְתָּ לִּירֵאֶיךָ (Tehillim 31:20), what You have stored up for those who fear You, and וּמִצְוֹתַי תִּצְפֹּן אִתָּךְ (Mishlei 2:1). All of them together, he says, are hiding and keeping out of sight.

נִצְפְּנָה לְנָקִי חִנָּם (Mishlei 1:11), let us lie in wait for the innocent without cause. His father reads that and יִצְפְּנוּ לְנַפְשֹׁתָם as saying the men hide themselves, setting themselves in a covert place.

וּצְפוּנְךָ תְּמַלֵּא בִטְנָם (Tehillim 17:14), the good stored with You to give to whom You please. The good of this world is called hidden, he says, because a man's hand does not reach it as he wishes but only as the Creator wills, so that what is good in his eyes is kept from him as though stored away. וְיִתְיָעֲצוּ עַל צְפוּנֶיךָ (Tehillim 83:4) he reads of Yisrael, hidden and sheltered under His wings.

more.h: Why the north is called צפון
more.t: He gives two reasons. Either because the settled world reaches only a little way into that quarter, so that it is as though hidden and unseen by men; or because the sun's path does not run on that side but on the southern one, so that the north is as it were hidden from the sun.

more.h: Why she hid them one by one
more.t: On אֶת שְׁנֵי הָאֲנָשִׁים וַתִּצְפְּנוֹ (Yehoshua 2:4) he notes the singular: Rachav did not hide the two men together in one place but each by himself, so that nobody should notice them. Or the singular may refer back to the word את, which takes in them both.

חבר.sense: To join together; whence חָבֵר, a companion, חַבּוּרָה, a bruise, and חֹבֵר חָבֶר, one who binds by charms.

more.t: כָּל אֵלֶּה חָבְרוּ (Bereishis 14:3), all these joined together, and שְׁתֵּי כְתֵפֹת חֹבְרֹת (Shemos 28:7). The nouns are חֶבֶר, a gathering, as חֶבֶר כֹּהֲנִים (Hoshea 6:9), and מַחְבֶּרֶת, a joining.
חָבֵר אָנִי לְכָל אֲשֶׁר יְרֵאוּךָ (Tehillim 119:63), I am a companion to all who fear You, and כְּאִישׁ אֶחָד חֲבֵרִים (Shoftim 20:11). The feminine is חֲבֶרֶת, as וְהִיא חֲבֶרְתְּךָ (Malachi 2:14).

וְחֹבֵר חָבֶר (Devarim 18:11), which he takes with Chazal in Sanhedrin: there is a great charmer and a small one. The great one whispers and gathers troops of large beasts; the small one whispers and gathers troops of small ones, such as snakes and scorpions.

חַבּוּרָה תַּחַת חַבּוּרָה (Shemos 21:25). A חבורה is a scratch or a gash, and from Chazal, he says, it appears to be the blow in which the blood is gathered without coming out; it is called חבורה because the blood is gathered at the place struck. Since it lies in the flesh like a stain, the leopard's spots are called חֲבַרְבֻּרֹתָיו (Yirmiyahu 13:23).

שֹרף.sense: To burn; whence שָׂרָף, the fiery serpent, and שְׂרָפִים, angels of fire.

more.t: וְשָׂרַף אֶת הַפָּרָה (Bamidbar 19:5). On וַיִּשְׂרֹף בָּאֵשׁ (Shemos 32:20) he notes that gold does not burn but melts: Moshe melted the calf in the fire to undo its form, and ground it afterwards.

וּבְמִשְׂרְפוֹת אֲבוֹתֶיךָ (Yirmiyahu 34:5). What is burnt for a king, he says with Chazal in Sanhedrin, is his bed and the vessels he used, and it is no way of the Emori. Others read the burning as a burning of spices over the dead so that the flesh should not stink.

עֲשֵׂה לְךָ שָׂרָף (Bamidbar 21:8) and הַנְּחָשִׁים הַשְּׂרָפִים: they are named so, he says, because they burn with the breath of their mouth. On שָׂרָף מְעוֹפֵף (Yeshayahu 14:29) he reports that winged serpents are said to be found in the land of Kush, or else that flying here means leaping far off, as though the creature were a bird.
שְׂרָפִים עֹמְדִים he glosses in two words: angels of fire.

הדר.sense: To honour and to give place to; הָדָר, splendour; and הֲדוּרִים, crooked ways.

more.t: וְהָדַרְתָּ פְּנֵי זָקֵן (Vayikra 19:32), you shall honour the face of an elder, and its opposite in judgment, וְדָל לֹא תֶהְדַּר בְּרִיבוֹ (Shemos 23:3), you shall not favour a poor man in his suit.

הָדוּר בִּלְבוּשׁוֹ (Yeshayahu 63:1), splendid in his garment, and פְּרִי עֵץ הָדָר (Vayikra 23:40), with the noun in הוֹד וְהָדָר לְפָנָיו (Tehillim 96:6). In the reflexive it is to make oneself fine: אַל תִּתְהַדַּר לִפְנֵי מֶלֶךְ (Mishlei 25:6), which he glosses as adorning and beautifying oneself and showing a pleasant face.
וַהֲדוּרִים he takes otherwise, as twisting and winding roads, and likens it to Chazal's הדרא דכנתא, the bowels, which turn round and round.

אדר.sense: Greatness and might: אַדִּיר, mighty, and אַדֶּרֶת, a mantle.

more.t: מָה אַדִּיר שִׁמְךָ (Tehillim 8:2), how mighty is Your name. Everything found from this root, he says, is a language of greatness and the strength of might, as יַגְדִּיל תּוֹרָה וְיַאְדִּיר (Yeshayahu 42:21).
בְּסֵפֶל אַדִּירִים (Shoftim 5:25) he reads as a bowl fit for great and honoured men to drink from, or else as the great shepherds, after אַדִּירֵי הַצֹּאן (Yirmiyahu 25:34).

On נֶאְדָּרִי בַּכֹּחַ (Shemos 15:6) Rabbi Yonah offers, among his explanations, that the tav of the feminine has fallen and the word is really נאדרית. Radak holds the first account the right one, that the yud is added.
כְּאַדֶּרֶת שֵׂעָר (Bereishis 25:25), a cloak of hair, and אַדֶּרֶת שִׁנְעָר (Yehoshua 7:21). It is called an אדרת, he says, for its worth and its greatness.

אגר.sense: To gather in; whence אִגֶּרֶת, a letter, and אֲגוֹרַת כֶּסֶף, a small coin.

more.t: אָגְרָה בַקָּצִיר מַאֲכָלָהּ (Mishlei 6:8), she gathers her food in the harvest, and וְיַיִן לֹא תִשְׁתֶּה וְלֹא תֶאֱגֹר (Devarim 28:39). Everything in Tanach from this root, he says, is gathering.
וְאִגֶּרֶת פְּתוּחָה (Nechemiah 6:5), an open letter. A scroll is called an אגרת from the same word, because many matters are gathered into it.
אַךְ לַאֲגוֹרַת כֶּסֶף (Shmuel I 2:36), a piece of silver, where the alef is added and the word is as גרה. The Targum renders it a maah of silver.

סלע.sense: A rock; and by transfer a stronghold, since strongholds are built upon rock.

more.t: וְדִבַּרְתֶּם אֶל הַסֶּלַע (Bamidbar 20:8), and סְלָעִים מַחְסֶה לַשְׁפַנִּים (Tehillim 104:18).

High fortresses are called סלע because most of them are built on rock: וְשִׂים בַּסֶּלַע קִנֶּךָ (Bamidbar 24:21), which the Targum renders as setting one's dwelling in a strong city. So too וְתָפַשׂ אֶת הַסֶּלַע בַּמִּלְחָמָה (Melachim II 14:6).

סַלְעִי וּמְצוּדָתִי (Tehillim 18:3), after the manner of מִגְדַּל עֹז שֵׁם (Mishlei 18:10). On וְסַלְעוֹ מִמָּגוֹר יַעֲבוֹר (Yeshayahu 31:9) the Targum reads סלעו as his king; Radak offers that it may be taken plainly, that out of terror he flees to his rock and his strong towers. His father explains it the other way: a man fleeing his enemy fears nothing once he has reached his stronghold, but before the lifting of Hashem's hand even his rock and his fortresses pass away in dread.

עגל.sense: Round; whence מַעְגָּל, a track or an encampment, עָגִיל, an earring, עֵגֶל, a calf, and עֲגָלָה, a wagon.

more.t: עָגֹל סָבִיב (Melachim I 7:35), round about, and מְרֻבָּעוֹת לֹא עֲגֻלּוֹת (Melachim I 7:31), square and not round.

וְשָׁאוּל שֹׁכֵב בַּמַּעְגָּל (Shmuel I 26:5), which he glosses as the place of the camp, named so because a camp is pitched in a ring. The same word is a path: יָשָׁר מַעְגַּל צַדִּיק תְּפַלֵּס (Yeshayahu 26:7), and בְמַעְגְּלֵי צֶדֶק (Tehillim 23:3).

more.h: The earring, the calf, the wagon
more.t: עָגִיל is an earring, טַבַּעַת עָגִיל וְכוּמָז (Bamidbar 31:50) and וַעֲגִילִים עַל אָזְנָיִךְ (Yechezkel 16:12). On עֶגְלָה מְשֻׁלֶּשֶׁת (Bereishis 15:9) he holds it means three calves and cannot mean one three years old, since at three years she would be called a פרה. And the wagon, עֲגָלָה, is named, he says, because it is round.

גזר.sense: To cut and to cut off; and by transfer to decree, since a decree is cut through and does not turn back.

more.t: גִּזְרוּ אֶת הַיֶּלֶד הַחַי (Melachim I 3:25), cut the living child in two, and לְגֹזֵר יַם סוּף לִגְזָרִים (Tehillim 136:13). The noun is בֵּין הַגְּזָרִים הָאֵלֶּה (Bereishis 15:17), between these pieces.

אֶל אֶרֶץ גְּזֵרָה (Vayikra 16:22), a land cut off from settlement and from growing things. The chamber called הַגִּזְרָה he explains as the one cut off from the house. And סַפִּיר גִּזְרָתָם (Eichah 4:7) he reads as though they had been cut out of sapphire, so clear were they.
וּבְמַגְזְרֹת הַבַּרְזֶל (Shmuel II 12:31), the saws with which wood is cut, or iron tools like them that cut.

Said of a thing so firm that it will not turn back: וְתִגְזַר אֹמֶר וְיָקָם לָךְ (Iyov 22:28), you shall decree a thing and it shall stand for you, and אֲשֶׁר נִגְזַר עָלֶיהָ (Esther 2:1), where the matter is cut through and will not be turned back again.

ערב.sense: To mingle; whence עֶרֶב, evening, and מַעֲרָב, the west. Also to be sweet or pleasing, to stand surety, עֲרָבָה a desert plain, and עַרְבֵי נָחַל, willows.

more.t: וַיִּתְעָרְבוּ בַגּוֹיִם (Tehillim 106:35), they mingled among the nations, with the noun עֵרֶב רַב (Shemos 12:38), the mixed multitude. All of it together, he says, is the mingling and joining of things one with another.

The hour after sunset is עֶרֶב because it is the time of darkness, when things mingle so that a man cannot tell one from another or set them apart. And since the evening divides the night from the day, the night itself is called ערב. בֵּין הָעַרְבָּיִם (Shemos 12:6) runs from the sun's turning westward until night: two evenings, he says, the first when the sun begins to turn and the second after it has set. The quarter where the sun sets is מַעֲרָב.

more.h: The woof, the raven, the swarm
more.t: הָעֵרֶב (Vayikra 13:52) is the woof, named because it mingles with the warp, the warp thread being fine and the woof thicker than it. עֹרֵב is the raven. And הֶעָרֹב (Shemos 8:17) he explains as gatherings of wild creatures of many kinds together.

מִנְחַת יְהוּדָה (Malachi 3:4) shall be עָרְבָה, pleasing and acceptable before Him; כִּי קוֹלֵךְ עָרֵב (Shir HaShirim 2:14), your voice is sweet. From this he takes the heavens being called עֲרָבוֹת, לָרֹכֵב בָּעֲרָבוֹת (Tehillim 68:5), because they are good and honoured.

כִּי עַבְדְּךָ עָרַב אֶת הַנַּעַר (Bereishis 44:32), your servant went surety for the boy, and the pledge itself, עֵרָבוֹן (Bereishis 38:17). On וְאֶת עֲרֻבָּתָם תִּקָּח (Shmuel I 17:18) he holds it means their pledge, since soldiers are used to pawning against their expenses, having no ready money with them.

Merchandise is called מַעֲרָב, he says, because merchants are used to mingling with one another in their trade. On וְאֶת הָעֹרְבִים צִוִּיתִי לְכַלְכֶּלְךָ שָׁם (Melachim I 17:4) three readings stand. Rabbi Yonah allows they may belong to the pleasing sense, Hashem having stirred men's spirits to sustain him; his father takes them from trade; and Radak holds the plain reading right, that they are ravens, the black unclean birds.

more.h: The plain, Arabia, and the willows
more.t: עֲרָבָה is a desert plain, בַּמִּדְבָּר בָּעֲרָבָה (Devarim 1:1) and בְּעַרְבוֹת מוֹאָב (Bamidbar 22:1). זְאֵב עֲרָבוֹת (Yirmiyahu 5:6) may be the wolf of the plain, or, he offers, the wolf of the evening, since wolves come to the city at night to tear, which is how Yonasan renders it, דֵיבֵי רַמְשָׁא. עֲרָב is Arabia, whose people dwell in the desert. And וְעַרְבֵי נָחַל (Vayikra 23:40) are willows.

קרב.sense: To draw near; whence קָרוֹב, near or a kinsman, קָרְבָּן, an offering, קֶרֶב, the inward part, and קְרָב, battle.

more.t: וְלֹא קָרַב זֶה אֶל זֶה כָּל הַלָּיְלָה (Shemos 14:20), the one did not come near the other all night, and קָרְבָה שְׁנַת הַשֶּׁבַע (Devarim 15:9), the seventh year has drawn near.

The adjective is קָרוֹב; it is also a kinsman, וְאִישׁ אֶת קְרֹבוֹ (Shemos 32:27), each man his kinsman, and בִּקְרֹבַי אֶקָּדֵשׁ (Vayikra 10:3). The noun is in קִרְבַת אֱלֹהִים לִי טוֹב (Tehillim 73:28), the nearness of Hashem is good for me.

Where the verb takes an object it is to bring near or to offer: וְהִקְרִיב הַכֹּהֵן אֶת הַכֹּל (Vayikra 1:13), and וּפַרְעֹה הִקְרִיב (Shemos 14:10), which he reads as Pharaoh bringing his camp near. What is brought upon the mizbeach is a קָרְבָּן.

קֶרֶב is what is within: וַתִּצְחַק שָׂרָה בְּקִרְבָּהּ (Bereishis 18:12), which he glosses as within her heart, and כִּי יָקוּם בְּקִרְבְּךָ נָבִיא (Devarim 13:2), in your midst. The entrails are called so because they are within, וְהַקֶּרֶב וְהַכְּרָעַיִם (Vayikra 1:13).

כְּיוֹם הִלָּחֲמוֹ בְּיוֹם קְרָב (Zechariah 14:3) and טוֹבָה חָכְמָה מִכְּלֵי קְרָב (Koheles 9:18). All of these, he says, are war, and the Targum of מלחמה is קרבא. On וּקֲרָב לִבּוֹ (Tehillim 55:22) he glosses: his mouth is smooth and his heart is war.

גלל.sense: To roll, and a long family that comes of rolling: גַּלְגַּל a wheel, מְגִלָּה a scroll, גֻּלְגֹּלֶת the skull, גַּל a heap or a wave, and גְּלִילוֹת, districts.

more.t: וְגָלֲלוּ אֶת הָאֶבֶן (Bereishis 29:3), they rolled the stone away. Of גֹּל אֶל, at Tehillim 22:9, he says: whoever turns his ways toward Hashem, He will deliver him.

The heavens are called גלגלים, with the letter doubled, because they go round the world continually. A wagon's wheel is a גַּלְגַּל, וְהָמַם גִּלְגַּל עֶגְלָתוֹ (Yeshayahu 28:28), and straw is called גַּלְגַּל because it rolls for its lightness, שִׁיתֵמוֹ כַגַּלְגַּל כְּקַשׁ לִפְנֵי רוּחַ (Tehillim 83:14).

more.h: The scroll, the skull, the heap
more.t: A letter is called a מְגִלָּה because it is rolled up, מְגִלָּה עָפָה (Zechariah 5:1). The head is a גֻּלְגֹּלֶת for its roundness, עֹמֶר לַגֻּלְגֹּלֶת (Shemos 16:16). A pile of stones is a גַּל for the same reason, עֵד הַגַּל הַזֶּה (Bereishis 31:52); and the sea's waves are גַּלִּים because they roll as they move.

Dung is called גָּלָל because it rolls, כְּגֶלְלוֹ לָנֶצַח יֹאבֵד (Iyov 20:7), and from this, he says, the idols are called גלולים, for their worthlessness and their filth. Chazal in Bava Kamma take the גלל of כַּאֲשֶׁר יְבַעֵר הַגָּלָל as the tooth, and the tooth is called גלל, he explains, because it is like the stone called אֶבֶן גְּלָל, which is marble.

גְּלִילוֹת הַיַּרְדֵּן (Yehoshua 22:10) and גְּלִיל הַגּוֹיִם (Yeshayahu 8:23), which he takes as a border, a region or a province. He ends by saying that everything falling under this root is one thing, though each word is explained according to its own place and what stands nearest it. And בִּגְלַל הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה (Devarim 15:10) is on account of this thing.

שׁבל.sense: שְׁבִיל, a path; שִׁבֹּלֶת, an ear of grain and also a rushing stream; and שַׁבְּלוּל, the snail.

more.t: שְׁבִילֵי עוֹלָם (Yirmiyahu 18:15), the ancient paths, and וּשְׁבִילְךָ בְּמַיִם רַבִּים (Tehillim 77:20).

חֶשְׂפִּי שֹׁבֶל (Yeshayahu 47:2) he takes as the leg or the thigh, since the pasuk goes on גַּלִּי שׁוֹק עִבְרִי נְהָרוֹת. The Midrash reads it from שבולת, the flowing of the river, and Rabbi Yonah reads it as uncover the locks of your hair, by way of likeness.

more.h: The ear of grain, and the stream
more.t: וָאֲלַקֳטָה בַשִּׁבֳּלִים (Rus 2:2), let me glean among the ears of grain. The same word is the rush of water, the place where water is carried down with force: אַל תִּשְׁטְפֵנִי שִׁבֹּלֶת מַיִם (Tehillim 69:16). That, he says, is why the test was אֱמָר נָא שִׁבֹּלֶת וַיֹּאמֶר סִבֹּלֶת (Shoftim 12:6): there was a rush of water at that place, and they tried a man by the thing that stood before him.

שַׁבְּלוּל תֶּמֶס יַהֲלֹךְ (Tehillim 58:9). He brings Chazal in Shabbos, that the Holy One created nothing in His world for nothing: He created the snail as a remedy for a sore, which is crushed and laid upon it.

עצם.sense: To be strong or numerous; עֶצֶם, a bone, and from it the body itself or a thing's very self; and to shut the eyes.

more.t: כִּי עָצַמְתָּ מִמֶּנּוּ (Bereishis 26:16), you have grown mightier than we, and רַב וְעָצוּם (Shemos 1:9). The nouns are עֹצֶם, as כֹּחִי וְעֹצֶם יָדִי (Devarim 8:18), and עָצְמָה. All of them together, he says, are strength, force and greatness.

It is said of the strength of a dispute as well: וּבֵין עֲצוּמִים יַפְרִיד (Mishlei 18:18), between those who press hard against one another in a quarrel, and הַגִּישׁוּ עֲצֻמוֹתֵיכֶם (Yeshayahu 41:21), the force of your suit and your proofs. He brings Chazal's usage in Sanhedrin, שנים שנתעצמו בדין, two who pressed one another at law.
עֶצֶם מֵעֲצָמַי (Bereishis 2:23), with the plurals עֲצָמִים and עַצְמוֹת. The bone is called so, he says, because it is stronger and firmer than the flesh.

more.h: The body, and a thing's own self
more.t: Since the bone is the strength of the body and holds it up, the body itself is called עצם: אַךְ עַצְמִי וּבְשָׂרִי אָתָּה (Bereishis 29:14). Where flesh is named beside it, he says, the bone does not mean bone alone but the body, and the flesh after it says the same thing twice; Chazal use עצם for the body often. From the same comes a thing's own self: בְּעֶצֶם הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה (Bereishis 7:13), the body of the day itself, and וּכְעֶצֶם הַשָּׁמַיִם לָטֹהַר (Shemos 24:10).
וְעֹצֵם עֵינָיו מֵרְאוֹת בְּרָע (Yeshayahu 33:15), and וַיְעַצֵּם אֶת עֵינֵיכֶם (Yeshayahu 29:10). Their sense, he says, is closing.

שׁור.sense: To sing; to look or to watch; תְּשׁוּרָה, a gift; שׁוּר, a wall; and שׁוֹר, an ox.

more.t: שָׁרִים וְשָׁרוֹת (Koheles 2:8), men singers and women singers, and אָז יָשִׁיר מֹשֶׁה (Shemos 15:1). The nouns are שִׁיר and שִׁירָה.

אֲשׁוּרֶנּוּ וְלֹא קָרוֹב (Bamidbar 24:17), I behold him but not near. יָשׁוּר כְּשַׁךְ יְקוּשִׁים (Yirmiyahu 5:26) he glosses: he watches as a man who sets a trap watches the birds until they settle, and so do they watch and lie in wait for men. Their sense, he says, is looking and observing, and from it אֱלֹהִים יַרְאֵנִי בְשֹׁרְרָי (Tehillim 59:11) means my enemies, since an enemy watches his enemy and observes him for harm.

וּתְשׁוּרָה אֵין לְהָבִיא (Shmuel I 9:7), a present. Rabbi Yonah reads וַתָּשֻׁרִי לַמֶּלֶךְ בַּשֶּׁמֶן (Yeshayahu 57:9) the same way, that you brought him a gift, and Rav Saadiah Gaon explains it so too; Radak holds the right reading is that ותשורי is as ותלכי, you went. A gift is called תשורה, he says, because a man carries it along with him.

אֳנִיּוֹת תַּרְשִׁישׁ שָׁרוֹתַיִךְ (Yechezkel 27:25), which he explains as the caravans that travel in trade; those who go by sea are called a caravan too, since many ships go together. He notes the Targum of אֹרְחַת יִשְׁמְעֵאלִים is שְׁיָרַת עֲרָבָאֵי.

בָּנוֹת צָעֲדָה עֲלֵי שׁוּר (Bereishis 49:22), where שׁוּר is a wall, as the Targum of חומה is שׁוּרִין. And שׁוֹר אוֹ כֶשֶׂב אוֹ עֵז (Vayikra 17:3), the ox. On עִקְּרוּ שׁוֹר (Bereishis 49:6) Rabbi Yaakov ben Elazar takes the ox as a figure for a ruler, as Tanach calls great princes rams and he-goats; others take it plainly, that they hamstrung the cattle.

שֹור.sense: To rule, whence שָׂרִים, princes; and מְשׂוּרָה, a very small measure.

more.t: שָׂרִים עָצְרוּ בְמִלִּים (Iyov 29:10), princes held back their words, and וַיָּשַׂר אֲבִימֶלֶךְ (Shoftim 9:22), Avimelech ruled. Where the verb takes an object it is to set someone in rule: הֵשִׂירוּ וְלֹא יָדָעְתִּי (Hoshea 8:4), they set up a prince over themselves and not by My leave.

בַּמִּשְׁקָל וּבַמְּשׂוּרָה (Vayikra 19:35). A מְשׂוּרָה is a measure, but a very small one: he brings Chazal in Bava Metzia, that it is a thirty-third part of a log. On וּמַיִם בִּמְשׂוּרָה תִשְׁתֶּה (Yechezkel 4:11) he warns that the measure is not itself a sixth of a hin; the pasuk means he shall drink no more than that in a day, and shall drink it little by little, by the measure. In וּלְכָל מְשׂוּרָה וּמִדָּה, he says, משורה is said of the small measures and מדה of the large.

וְשָׂם חִטָּה שׂוֹרָה (Yeshayahu 28:25) some take from ruling, that the wheat is fine and choice. Rabbi Yonah sets it with the measures instead, since the pasuk goes on to name barley and spelt by their places.

הלך.sense: To go and to walk; whence הֲלִיכָה, a going, מַהֲלַךְ, a day's distance, and הֵלֶךְ, a wayfarer.

more.t: הֹלֵךְ לִקְרָאתְךָ (Bereishis 32:7), coming to meet you, and וַתִּהֲלַךְ אֵשׁ (Shemos 9:23), fire went along the ground. The noun is הֲלִיכָה, with the plural הֲלִיכוֹת עוֹלָם לוֹ (Chavakuk 3:6).
מַהֲלַךְ יוֹם (Yonah 3:4), a day's journey; and הֵלֶךְ, a traveller, וַיָּבֹא הֵלֶךְ לְאִישׁ הֶעָשִׁיר (Shmuel II 12:4).

הִתְהַלֵּךְ לְפָנַי וֶהְיֵה תָמִים (Bereishis 17:1), and what is said of Noach and of the avos, אֲשֶׁר הִתְהַלְּכוּ אֲבֹתַי לְפָנָיו (Bereishis 48:15). He glosses the reflexive here as occupying oneself in the service of Hashem.

חפץ.sense: To desire and to delight in; the noun חֵפֶץ, a desire, or the thing desired.

more.t: כִּי חָפֵץ בְּבַת יַעֲקֹב (Bereishis 34:19), he delighted in Yaakov's daughter, and וְאִם לֹא יַחְפֹּץ הָאִישׁ (Devarim 25:7). The noun is חֵפֶץ, and in the plural וְכָל חֲפָצֶיךָ לֹא יִשְׁווּ בָהּ (Mishlei 3:15), all your desires are not to be weighed against her.
On דְּרוּשִׁים לְכָל חֶפְצֵיהֶם (Tehillim 111:2) he holds the right reading is that חפציהם describes people rather than things: they are sought out by all who desire them.

יַחְפֹּץ זְנָבוֹ כְמוֹ אָרֶז (Iyov 40:17) he reports is explained as a sense of movement, the tzadi standing in for a zayin, the two coming from one place in the mouth, as לֹא יַחְפּוֹז (Iyov 40:23), which is moving quickly. The meaning is that his tail, great as a cedar, he moves swiftly.

חפר.sense: To dig, and close to it to search out; a second sense is to be ashamed.

more.t: כִּי חָפַרְתִּי אֶת הַבְּאֵר הַזֹּאת (Bereishis 21:30), I dug this well, and חֲפָרוּהָ שָׂרִים (Bamidbar 21:18). On וְחָפַרְתָּ לָבֶטַח תִּשְׁכָּב (Iyov 11:18) he explains that you will need only to dig round your buildings and will not have to wall them or raise them up, since you will lie down in safety.

כִּי לַחְפֹּר אֶת כָּל הָאָרֶץ בָּאוּ (Yehoshua 2:2), they have come to search out the whole land, and מִשָּׁם חָפַר אֹכֶל (Iyov 39:29). It is searching and seeking, he says, because one who searches for a thing is like one who digs for it.

לַחְפֹּר פֵּרוֹת (Yeshayahu 2:20) Rabbi Yonah takes as the name of a bird, called so for its much pecking at fruit; Radak allows it, since bats are named beside it in the pasuk and men made images of birds and bats to bow down to. He offers as well that it may be two words meaning to dig diggings, men hiding themselves in holes as bats hide by day, since the pasuk goes on לָבוֹא בְּנִקְרוֹת הַצֻּרִים.

וְחָפְרָה הַלְּבָנָה (Yeshayahu 24:23), the moon shall be abashed, and וּבֹשׁוּ הַחֹזִים וְחָפְרוּ הַקֹּסְמִים (Michah 3:7). All of these, he says, are shame, and הֶחְפִּיר לְבָנוֹן (Yeshayahu 33:9) is said by way of figure, after the manner of הַגֶּפֶן הוֹבִישָׁה (Yoel 1:12).

יבל.sense: To carry or bring; יוּבַל, a stream; יְבוּל, the land's produce; and יוֹבֵל, a ram's horn and the fiftieth year.

more.t: מִי יֹבִלֵנִי עִיר מָצוֹר (Tehillim 60:11), who will bring me to the fortified city, and יוּבַל שַׁי (Yeshayahu 18:7). Their sense, he says, is bringing, and he notes that the Targum renders bringing by this root.

וְעַל יוּבַל יְשַׁלַּח שָׁרָשָׁיו (Yirmiyahu 17:8), which he glosses as a channel of water, and פְּלָגִים יִבְלֵי מָיִם (Yeshayahu 30:25), where the pasuk says streams first and then explains that they are streams of water.

וְנָתְנָה הָאָרֶץ יְבוּלָהּ (Vayikra 26:4), the land shall give her produce, and וְאֵין יְבוּל בַּגְּפָנִים (Chavakuk 3:17). Their sense, he says, is crops and fruit and everything the ground brings forth.

more.h: Why the year is called יובל
more.t: The Targum renders קֶרֶן הַיּוֹבֵל as horns of rams, and Chazal in Rosh Hashanah ask how יובל means a ram: Rabbi Akiva said that when he went to Arabia he heard them call a ram יובלא. The shofar itself is called יובל because it is made of a ram's horn, and the fiftieth year is called יובל because a ram's horn is blown in it, יוֹבֵל הִוא תִּהְיֶה לָכֶם (Vayikra 25:10).
אוֹ חָרוּץ אוֹ יַבֶּלֶת (Vayikra 22:22). He notes that in the pasuk יבלת describes the animal that has one, as חרוץ does, while in the Mishnah it is the name of the thing itself.

סתר.sense: To be hidden, and to hide; the noun סֵתֶר, a hiding place or secrecy.

more.t: נִסְתְּרָה דַרְכִּי (Yeshayahu 40:27), my way is hidden, and אִם יִסָּתֵר אִישׁ בַּמִּסְתָּרִים (Yirmiyahu 23:24), if a man hide himself in secret places.

אַסְתִּירָה פָנַי מֵהֶם (Devarim 32:20), I will hide My face from them, and בְּאַשְׁפָּתוֹ הִסְתִּירָנִי (Yeshayahu 49:2). On וְחַטֹּאותֵיכֶם הִסְתִּירוּ פָנִים מִכֶּם מִשְּׁמוֹעַ (Yeshayahu 59:2) he notes that the verb there carries two objects.
אַתָּה סֵתֶר לִי מִצַּר (Tehillim 32:7), You are a hiding place for me from trouble, and בַּמִּסְתָּרִים יַהֲרֹג נָקִי (Tehillim 10:8), in the hiding places he kills the innocent.

more.h: A word written with a sin
more.t: וַיִּשָּׂתְרוּ לָהֶם (Shmuel I 5:9): though it is written with a sin, he says it is one sense with this root, and explains that the tumours were covered over within them.

On וְסֵתֶר מַיִם יִשְׁטֹפוּ (Yeshayahu 28:17) he offers that סתר may stand in construct with the water, and be taken in the sense Chazal use often in Bava Kamma, of pulling down, as in הסותר את כותלו, one who pulls down his wall.

נסך.sense: Three senses: to cover over, whence מַסֵּכָה, a covering and an overlaid idol; to pour or to cast, whence נֶסֶךְ, a libation; and to install as a prince.

more.t: כִּי נָסַךְ עֲלֵיכֶם, He has poured over you רוּחַ תַּרְדֵּמָה, a spirit of deep sleep (Yeshayahu 29:10), and וְהַמַּסֵּכָה הַנְּסוּכָה (Yeshayahu 25:7). All of these, he says, are hiding and covering. הַמַּסֵּכָה and הַמַּסָּכֶת (Shoftim 16:14) he takes as the name of the cloth spread over a bed.
הַפֶּסֶל נָסַךְ חָרָשׁ (Yeshayahu 40:19) and כִּי שֶׁקֶר נִסְכּוֹ (Yirmiyahu 10:14) he reads from the covering sense, because they made the image of wood and overlaid it with gold and silver.

וְאֵת קְשׂוֹת הַנָּסֶךְ (Bamidbar 4:7) he explains as the tubes with which it is covered: they were like hollow half reeds set over each loaf so that air should pass between them and the bread not go mouldy, and so the tubes were a cover over the bread.
וְנֵסֶךְ לֹא תִסְּכוּ עָלָיו (Shemos 30:9), you shall pour no libation upon it, and וְהִסִּכוּ נְסָכִים (Yirmiyahu 32:29). All of these, he says, are pouring and melting.

וַאֲנִי נָסַכְתִּי מַלְכִּי (Tehillim 2:6), I have set My king, and נְסִיכֵי סִיחוֹן (Yehoshua 13:21). All of these, he says, are greatness, rule and princedom. He offers וְלִנְסֹךְ מַסֵּכָה וְלֹא רוּחִי (Yeshayahu 30:1) in this sense as well, that they set rulers over themselves without His leave, seeking help from Pharaoh; or else in the first sense, as a figure for taking counsel.

ירח.sense: יָרֵחַ, the moon; and יֶרַח, a month, since the moon renews itself each month.

more.t: עָשָׂה יָרֵחַ לְמוֹעֲדִים (Tehillim 104:19), He made the moon for appointed times, and וְיָרֵחַ לֹא יַגִּיהַ אוֹרוֹ (Yeshayahu 13:10), which he glosses: the moon shall not give its light.

Because the moon renews itself every month, the month is called יֶרַח: בְּיֶרַח הָאֵתָנִים (Melachim I 8:2) and מִי יִתְּנֵנִי כְיַרְחֵי קֶדֶם (Iyov 29:2). And because it renews itself many times it is spoken of in the plural although it is only one, גֶּרֶשׁ יְרָחִים (Devarim 33:14), which he explains as the moon ripening the fruits.

ירשׁ.sense: To inherit and to take possession; where the verb takes an object with מן, to drive out; and תִּירוֹשׁ, new wine.

more.t: וְיָרַשְׁנוּ אֹתָהּ (Bamidbar 13:30), we shall take possession of it, and וִירִשְׁתֶּם אֹתָהּ וִישַׁבְתֶּם בָּהּ (Devarim 11:31). All of them are one sense, he says: some are a son's inheritance from his father, and some the taking of a thing out of another's hand, that is, taking his inheritance and what was in his holding, as a son takes his father's estate.

וּבְנֵי עֵשָׂו יִירָשׁוּם (Devarim 2:12) he reads plainly, that they took their inheritance, and says there is no need to take it out of the sense of inheriting as Rabbi Yonah did, who explained it as driving out.

מוֹרִישׁ אוֹתָם מִפָּנֶיךָ (Devarim 18:12), driving them out before you, and וְאִם לֹא תוֹרִישׁוּ אֶת יֹשְׁבֵי הָאָרֶץ מִפְּנֵיכֶם (Bamidbar 33:55). The rule, he says, is that wherever the word is bound to a מ it is driving out and sending away. He then allows that even לָרֶשֶׁת אוֹתָם מִפָּנֶיךָ (Devarim 12:29) may be inheriting, the מפניך belonging to כִּי יַכְרִית rather than to לרשת, and on that reading no simple form of the verb means driving out at all.
פֶּן תִּוָּרֵשׁ (Bereishis 45:11) and וּפֶן אִוָּרֵשׁ וְגָנַבְתִּי (Mishlei 30:9), which he glosses as poverty and want; so too Targum Yonasan on הַלְיָרְשֵׁנוּ קְרָאתֶם לָנוּ (Shoftim 14:15).
From this same root, he says, comes a noun that belongs to none of those senses: הַתִּירוֹשׁ, as כַּאֲשֶׁר יִמָּצֵא הַתִּירוֹשׁ בָּאֶשְׁכּוֹל (Yeshayahu 65:8). It is the new wine.

שֹרק.sense: שׂוֹרֵק, the choicest kind of vine; and שְׂרֻקִּים, of horses, patterned or combed.

more.t: נְטַעְתִּיךְ שׂוֹרֵק (Yirmiyahu 2:21), I planted you a choice vine, and וְלַשֹּׂרֵקָה בְּנִי אֲתֹנוֹ (Bereishis 49:11). It is the best of the kinds of vine; Rav Yitzchak ibn Giat writes that it is the good kind whose grapes have no stone in them, and Targum Yonasan renders it a choice vine.

שְׂרֻקִּים וּלְבָנִים (Zechariah 1:8) he explains as patterned, their colour red and white and black as though they were speckled or dappled, and so עֹבְדֵי פִשְׁתִּים שְׂרִיקוֹת (Yeshayahu 19:9), worked in colours. He brings Chazal's לובשי סריקין של זהב, garments figured with gold. Others take שְׂרֻקִּים as combed out, and he brings Chazal in Moed Katan, that Rava permitted the combing of a horse with an iron comb.

שׁרק.sense: To whistle or hiss, which he glosses as the moving of the lips in sound.

more.t: וְשָׁרַק לוֹ מִקְצֵה הָאָרֶץ (Yeshayahu 5:26), He will whistle to him from the end of the earth, and אֶשְׁרְקָה לָהֶם וַאֲקַבְּצֵם (Zechariah 10:8), I will whistle to them and gather them.
שָׁרְקוּ וַיָּנִעוּ רֹאשָׁם (Eichah 2:15), they hissed and wagged their head, and וְיֹשְׁבֶיהָ לִשְׁרֵקָה (Michah 6:16). The noun is also of flocks, שְׁרִקוֹת עֲדָרִים (Shoftim 5:16).

סוס.sense: סוּס, a horse, with סוּסָה for the mare; and a bird of the same name.

more.t: כִּי בָא סוּס פַּרְעֹה (Shemos 15:19), and the feminine לְסֻסָתִי בְּרִכְבֵי פַרְעֹה (Shir HaShirim 1:9). On דָּרַכְתָּ בַיָּם סוּסֶיךָ (Chavakuk 3:15) he says the horses are a figure for the clouds.

A bird carries the same name: כְּסוּס עָגוּר כֵּן אֲצַפְצֵף (Yeshayahu 38:14), which he reads as two birds, like a סוס and a עגור, after the manner of שֶׁמֶשׁ יָרֵחַ (Chavakuk 3:11), where two are named without an and between them. Elsewhere the same bird is written with a yud in place of the vav, וְסִיס, standing between the turtledove and the crane (Yirmiyahu 8:7).

נהר.sense: To stream toward a thing; whence נָהָר, a river, the place where water runs. A second sense is to shine, whence נְהָרָה, light.

more.t: וְנָהֲרוּ אֵלָיו כָּל הַגּוֹיִם (Yeshayahu 2:2), all the nations shall stream to it, and וְלֹא יִנְהֲרוּ אֵלָיו עוֹד גּוֹיִם (Yirmiyahu 51:44). Their sense, he says, is running toward the thing desired.

From that the river is named, being the place where the water runs: נָהָר פְּלָגָיו (Tehillim 46:5) and בְּעֵבֶר הַנָּהָר (Yehoshua 24:2), with the plurals נְהָרִים and נַהֲרוֹת, as עַל נַהֲרוֹת בָּבֶל (Tehillim 137:1).

הִבִּיטוּ אֵלָיו וְנָהָרוּ (Tehillim 34:6), they looked to Him and were radiant, and אָז תִּרְאִי וְנָהַרְתְּ (Yeshayahu 60:5); the noun is וְאַל תּוֹפַע עָלָיו נְהָרָה (Iyov 3:4). Their sense, he says, is light, and he notes that the Targum of אור is נְהוֹרָא. Some read וְנָהֲרוּ אֵלָיו in this sense rather than the first.

הַמִּנְהָרוֹת אֲשֶׁר בֶּהָרִים (Shoftim 6:2) are caves, and he says they are named with a word of light because of the opening through which the light comes in, as a serpent's den is called מְאוּרַת צִפְעוֹנִי (Yeshayahu 11:8) in the same way.

אבל.sense: To mourn, whence אֵבֶל, mourning; a second sense of lying waste; and the separate word אֲבָל.

more.t: כִּי אָבַל עָלָיו עַמּוֹ (Hoshea 10:5), his people mourned over him, and וַיִּתְאַבֵּל עַל בְּנוֹ (Bereishis 37:34). The noun is אֵבֶל כָּבֵד זֶה לְמִצְרָיִם (Bereishis 50:11). On כַּאֲבֶל אֵם (Tehillim 35:14) his father explains the figure: as an infant whose mother nursed him and died, who weeps and is darkened because he has nobody to nurse him, his mother's breasts having been his life, so was he darkened and bowed down.

more.h: How to tell the second sense
more.t: Some uses are desolation and ruin rather than grief: עַל כֵּן תֶּאֱבַל הָאָרֶץ וְאֻמְלַל כָּל יוֹשֵׁב בָּהּ (Hoshea 4:3). Whenever you find the word bound to אֻמְלַל, he says, it is ruin and waste and destruction, as אָבַל תִּירוֹשׁ אֻמְלְלָה גָפֶן (Yeshayahu 24:7); and all the rest are mourning.

more.h: The great stone at Beis Shemesh
more.t: וְעַד אָבֵל הַגְּדוֹלָה אֲשֶׁר הִנִּיחוּ עָלֶיהָ (Shmuel I 6:18) some explain as the great plain, since the Targum of אָבֵל מְחוֹלָה is a plain; others that the lamed stands for a nun and it is the great stone on which they set the Aron, which is how Targum Yonasan renders it. Radak gives his own view: the stone's name was אָבֵל, called so for the mourning that was made at it, as the threshing floor of Atad was called אָבֵל מִצְרַיִם for the same reason.

One word of this root is neither verb nor noun but a particle, and he separates two uses. In אֲבָל שָׂרָה אִשְׁתְּךָ (Bereishis 17:19) and אֲבָל בֵּן אֵין לָהּ (Melachim II 4:14) it means not this alone but this also, or not this but that; he works both through at length from what stands above them. In אֲבָל אֲשֵׁמִים אֲנַחְנוּ (Bereishis 42:21) and אֲבָל אִשָּׁה אַלְמָנָה אָנִי (Shmuel II 14:5) it means truly. Which of the two is meant, he says, a reader can tell from what is written above it.

אסר.sense: To bind and to tie; whence אָסִיר, a prisoner, and בֵּית הָאֵסוּר, the prison.

more.t: וַיֶּאְסֹר אֶת רִכְבּוֹ (Shemos 14:6), he harnessed his chariot, and וַאֲסַרְנֻהוּ לְעַנֹּתוֹ (Shoftim 16:5). All of them, he says, are binding, and מִי יֶאְסֹר הַמִּלְחָמָה (Melachim I 20:14) he explains as the harnessing of the chariot.
וְאָסְרָה אִסָּר (Bamidbar 30:4), and she binds a bond upon herself.

אֶנְקַת אָסִיר (Tehillim 79:11), the groaning of the prisoner, with the plural הָאֲסִירִם אֲשֶׁר בְּבֵית הַסֹּהַר (Bereishis 39:22). The prison is בֵּית הָאֵסוּר (Yirmiyahu 37:15), and he notes that in מִבֵּית הָסוּרִים (Koheles 4:14) the alef is silent and left out of the writing. אֲסוּרִים יָדֶיהָ (Koheles 7:26) he glosses as one caught in her hands, like a man shut up in the prison house.
Rabbi Yehudah holds that בְּמָסֹרֶת הַבְּרִית (Yechezkel 20:37) belongs to this root, the word being properly בְּמַאֲסֹרֶת.

נגד.sense: To tell; נֶגֶד, opposite or in front of; and נָגִיד, the head of a people.

more.t: מִי הִגִּיד לְךָ (Bereishis 3:11). All of them, he says, are a sense of relating, except in this: telling is said of news as well, while relating is said only of a thing that was done or said.

נֶגֶד is in front of and over against. אֶעֱשֶׂה לּוֹ עֵזֶר כְּנֶגְדּוֹ (Bereishis 2:18) he glosses as one who should be before him and over against him always, to serve him. With a mem before it the word means at a distance: וַתֵּשֶׁב לָהּ מִנֶּגֶד (Bereishis 20:16), and מִנֶּגֶד נִגְעִי יַעֲמֹדוּ (Tehillim 38:12), standing far off over against me and not drawing near to visit me.

more.h: Why a ruler is called נגיד
more.t: From this, he says, the head of the people is called נָגִיד, וְאַתָּה תִּהְיֶה לְנָגִיד (Shmuel II 5:2), because the people set their faces toward him always and turn to him in all their affairs. Good and wise words are called נְגִידִים for the same reason, שִׁמְעוּ כִּי נְגִידִים אֲדַבֵּר (Mishlei 8:6), because all turn toward them for their worth.

more.h: A pasuk with a word left out
more.t: On נָגִיד חֲסַר תְּבוּנוֹת וְרַב מַעֲשַׁקּוֹת (Mishlei 28:16) he says the end of the pasuk teaches the beginning: the word ימות is missing and left for the reader to supply, as Tanach often leaves out what can be understood from what stands beside it. His father reads it from the Targum instead, either that a man full of oppressions is drawn out of the world, or better, that he dies before his time.

בער.sense: To burn, said of the fire itself; to clear away; to graze a field bare; בְּעִיר, a beast; and בַּעַר, a brutish man.

more.h: How burning differs from burning up
more.t: וְהִנֵּה הַסְּנֶה בֹּעֵר בָּאֵשׁ (Shemos 3:2), which he glosses as alight. Burning and burning up are both kindling and consuming, he says, except in this: burning is said of the fire itself, even where its working does not pass on to another, while burning up always has its working pass to something else.

Some hold that every form of בוער carries an object, and he asks what they will do with כַּפִּשְׁתִּים אֲשֶׁר בָּעֲרוּ בָאֵשׁ (Shoftim 15:14), which were themselves burnt. The right account, he says, is that all the simple forms stand without an object, and כְּאֵשׁ תִּבְעַר יָעַר (Tehillim 83:15) means burns in the forest.

וּבִעַרְתָּ הָרָע מִקִּרְבֶּךָ (Devarim 13:6), you shall clear away the evil from your midst, and בִּעַרְתִּי הַקֹּדֶשׁ מִן הַבַּיִת (Devarim 26:13). Their sense is cutting off and removal, he says, and it lies near the first.

כִּי יַבְעֶר אִישׁ שָׂדֶה אוֹ כֶרֶם (Shemos 22:4) he glosses as grazing, and בִּעַרְתֶּם הַכֶּרֶם (Yeshayahu 3:14), you have grazed the vineyard bare. This too lies near the first, he says, since grazing and eating are themselves a consuming.

טַעֲנוּ אֶת בְּעִירְכֶם (Bereishis 45:17), load your cattle, and he notes that the Targum of בהמה is בְּעִירָא. אִישׁ בַּעַר לֹא יֵדָע (Tehillim 92:7) lies near it, he says, because the fool is like a beast.

גבר.sense: To prevail and to be strong; whence גְּבוּרָה, might, גִּבּוֹר, a mighty man, גְּבִירָה, a mistress, and גֶּבֶר, a man.

more.t: גָּבַר חַסְדּוֹ עַל יְרֵאָיו (Tehillim 103:11), His kindness prevailed over those who fear Him, and וְהַמַּיִם גָּבְרוּ (Bereishis 7:19), the waters prevailed. All of them, he says, are strength, firmness and victory.

more.h: Why a man is called גבר
more.t: A man is called גֶּבֶר, he says, because he has strength over the woman: וְדֶרֶךְ גֶּבֶר בְּעַלְמָה (Mishlei 30:19). He notes that locusts are spoken of the same way, גֶּבֶר בִּמְסִלָּתוֹ יֵלֵכוּן (Yoel 2:8), because they are likened to men and to mighty ones.
הֵן גְּבִיר שַׂמְתִּיו לָךְ (Bereishis 27:37), which he glosses as a master and a head; and the feminine, שָׂרַי גְּבִרְתִּי (Bereishis 16:8) and גְּבֶרֶת מַמְלָכוֹת (Yeshayahu 47:5).

וַחֲיָלִים יְגַבֵּר (Koheles 10:10) he reads of a blunt axe: the man cleaving with it must put out the more strength. On טַלְטֵלָה גָּבֶר (Yeshayahu 22:17) he brings Chazal in Kesubos, that the tossing about of a man is harder to bear than the tossing about of a woman.

קצר.sense: To be short, the opposite of long; קָצִיר, a bough; and to reap, whence קָצִיר, the harvest.

more.t: כִּי קָצַר הַמַּצָּע (Yeshayahu 28:20), the bed is too short, and קָצְרָה יָדִי מִפְּדוּת (Yeshayahu 50:2). The noun is מִקֹּצֶר רוּחַ (Shemos 6:9), and the adjectives קְצַר יָמִים וּשְׂבַע רֹגֶז (Iyov 14:1) and קְצַר אַפַּיִם יַעֲשֶׂה אִוֶּלֶת (Mishlei 14:17). All of them together, he says, are straitness and shortness, which is the opposite of length.
וְעָשָׂה קָצִיר כְּמוֹ נָטַע (Iyov 14:9) and תְּשַׁלַּח קְצִירֶהָ עַד יָם (Tehillim 80:12), whose sense, he says, is a branch.
וּקְצַרְתֶּם אֶת קְצִירָהּ (Vayikra 23:10), you shall reap its harvest, with the noun בֶּחָרִישׁ וּבַקָּצִיר (Shemos 34:21), in plowing time and in harvest.

רעה.sense: To graze and to shepherd; to keep company, whence רֵעַ, a friend; רַעְיוֹן, a thought or a will; and a fourth sense, to break.

more.t: וְרָעוּ כְבָשִׂים (Yeshayahu 5:17), and where the verb takes two objects, הָאֱלֹהִים הָרֹעֶה אֹתִי (Bereishis 48:15). The flock itself is called מַרְעִית, as וְכָל מַרְעִיתָם נָפוֹצָה (Yirmiyahu 10:21), or else the place of pasture; and the pasture is מִרְעֶה שָׁמֵן וָטוֹב (Divrei HaYamim I 4:40).

וְרֹעֶה כְסִילִים (Mishlei 13:20), one who keeps company with fools, and וְרֹעֶה זוֹנוֹת (Mishlei 29:3). From this come מֵרֵעַ, a companion, as אֲשֶׁר רֵעָה לוֹ (Shoftim 14:20); the feminine רַעְיָתִי יָפָתִי (Shir HaShirim 2:10); and וְאִשָּׁה רְעוּתָהּ (Yirmiyahu 9:19), a woman and her neighbour.

וּבְרַעְיוֹן לִבּוֹ (Koheles 2:22) and בַּנְתָּה לְרֵעִי (Tehillim 139:2). All of them, he says, are will and thought, after the Targum's word for will. He reads וְלִי מַה יָּקְרוּ רֵעֶיךָ (Tehillim 139:17) against the pasuk above it: You understand my will and my thought from afar, before ever I think it, but Your will and Your thoughts are precious to me, since I cannot know them.

רֹעֶה עֲקָרָה לֹא תֵלֵד (Iyov 24:21) and יִרְעוּךְ קָדְקֹד (Yirmiyahu 2:16), whose sense, he says, is breaking. He allows that כָּל רֹעַיִךְ תִּרְעֶה רוּחַ (Yirmiyahu 22:22) may belong here, the wind they chase after breaking them.

וּרְעוּת רוּחַ (Koheles 1:14) he reports read three ways in the course of the entry, and does not choose between them: from grazing, after אֶפְרַיִם רֹעֶה רוּחַ (Hoshea 12:2), a feeding that neither profits nor satisfies; from will and thought; or from breaking.

נשֹא.sense: To carry, to bear, to lift, and to take; whence נָשִׂיא, a prince, מַשָּׂא, a burden and also a prophecy, and the forgiving of sin.

more.t: וְלֹא נָשָׂא אֹתָם הָאָרֶץ (Bereishis 13:6), which he glosses as the land not bearing them. He says plainly that everything entering this root enters one sense, carrying and taking, and that a reader can tell them apart easily enough each in its own place, so he will not set them out one by one. Lifting is וַיִּשָּׂא עֵינָיו וַיַּרְא (Bereishis 18:2) and וַיִּשָּׂא יַעֲקֹב רַגְלָיו (Bereishis 29:1); taking is וַיִּשְׂאוּ לָהֶם נָשִׁים מֹאֲבִיּוֹת (Rus 1:4), and he notes Chazal say בתולה נשאת in the same way.
A great man is a נָשִׂיא, וְנָשִׂיא בְעַמְּךָ לֹא תָאֹר (Shemos 22:27). The clouds are called נְשִׂיאִים for their rising up, מַעֲלֶה נְשִׂאִים (Tehillim 135:7).

וּמַשֹּׂא פָנִים (Divrei HaYamim II 19:7). He explains the figure: one who sins and is ashamed has his face fall, as וְלָמָּה נָפְלוּ פָנֶיךָ (Bereishis 4:6), and one who shows him a pleasant face is as though lifting up the face that had fallen.
שָׂא נָא חַטָּאתִי (Shemos 10:17) and אַשְׁרֵי נְשׂוּי פֶּשֶׁע (Tehillim 32:1). The forgiving of a sin, he says, is the lifting of it and the taking of it off the man.

more.h: Why a prophecy is a burden
more.t: A prophecy is called מַשָּׂא because it is borne in a man's mouth. On מַה מַשָּׂא (Yirmiyahu 23:33) he reads the exchange closely: when they asked the navi that, they did not mean prophecy but heaviness and burden, as in מַשָּׂא בְנֵי קְהָת (Bamidbar 4:15), the word of Hashem having become a heavy load to them. He who knows what is hidden revealed their thought to the navi, and so the answer came, כִּי הַמַּשָּׂא יִהְיֶה לְאִישׁ דְּבָרוֹ (Yirmiyahu 23:36): a man's own word is his burden, since it is carried in his mouth, and that is why prophecy is called מַשָּׂא, while you turn the words of Hashem and mean heaviness by them.

וַיִּשָּׂאֵם דָּוִד וַאֲנָשָׁיו (Shmuel II 5:21) he glosses as burning them, and the beacon is a מַשְׂאֵת; Chazal say משיאין משואות in the same way. It may be called so, he suggests, for the flame that rises up.

נשׁא.sense: To entice and to lead astray; and a second sense, ruin and desolation.

more.t: הַנָּחָשׁ הִשִּׁיאַנִי (Bereishis 3:13), the serpent enticed me, and אַל יַשִּׁיא לָכֶם חִזְקִיָּהוּ (Melachim II 18:29). All of these, he says, are leading astray and beguiling.
הַשֵּׁאת וְהַשָּׁבֶר (Eichah 3:47), and הִפַּלְתָּם לְמַשּׁוּאוֹת (Tehillim 73:18), with תִּכַּסֶּה שִׂנְאָה בְּמַשָּׁאוֹן (Mishlei 26:26). Their sense, he says, is waste and desolation.

כסה.sense: To cover; whence כְּסוּת, a covering or a garment, and מִכְסֶה, a covering over.

more.t: כִּסָּה הֶעָנָן (Bamidbar 9:15), the cloud covered it, and כִּי תִרְאֶה עָרֹם וְכִסִּיתוֹ (Yeshayahu 58:7), when you see the naked, cover him. In the reflexive, וַתִּקַּח הַצָּעִיף וַתִּתְכָּס (Bereishis 24:65), she took the veil and covered herself.
כְּסוּי עוֹר תַּחַשׁ (Bamidbar 4:6); כְּסוּת, as עַל אַרְבַּע כַּנְפוֹת כְּסוּתְךָ (Devarim 22:12) and כִּי הִוא כְסוּתֹה לְבַדָּהּ (Shemos 22:26); and וְעָשִׂיתָ מִכְסֶה לָאֹהֶל (Shemos 26:14).

אָדָם עָרוּם כֹּסֶה דָּעַת (Mishlei 12:23), a prudent man conceals knowledge. On אֵלֶיךָ כִסִּתִי (Tehillim 143:9) he reads the whole pasuk: I did not uncover my quarrel to men, since the help of man is vain, but hid it from them and uncovered it to You alone; and that, he says, is the sense of the words: I cried to You in secret and covered from men.

קנה.sense: To acquire and to buy; whence מִקְנֶה, cattle, a man's own possession. A second sense is קָנֶה, a reed, and the many things shaped like one.

more.t: אֲשֶׁר קָנָה אַבְרָהָם (Bereishis 25:10), and כִּי תִקְנֶה עֶבֶד עִבְרִי (Shemos 21:2). It stands against selling, he says; but there is an acquiring where there is no sale and no money paid, as קֹנֵה שָׁמַיִם וָאָרֶץ (Bereishis 14:19). Of מִקְנֶה וְקִנְיָן (Yechezkel 38:12) he says the one word is of the animals and the other of the rest of a man's goods.
The larger and smaller beasts are called מִקְנֶה, he says, because they are a man's possession and his money and his business: וּמִקְנֶה רַב הָיָה (Bamidbar 32:1).

more.h: The reed, and what is shaped like it
more.t: כַּאֲשֶׁר יָנוּד הַקָּנֶה (Melachim I 14:15), as the reed shakes. Because a reed is used for measuring, a measuring rod is a קָנֶה, בִּקְנֵה הַמִּדָּה (Yechezkel 42:17). The branches of the menorah are called קָנִים for the same likeness, וְשִׁשָּׁה קָנִים (Shemos 25:32); so is the upper arm, וְאֶזְרֹעִי מִקָּנָה תִשָּׁבֵר (Iyov 31:22), which he places from the elbow to the shoulder; so are spears, which is how he reads גְּעַר חַיַּת קָנֶה (Tehillim 68:31), the company that fights with spears; and so is the beam of a balance from which the pans hang, וְכֶסֶף בַּקָּנֶה יִשְׁקֹלוּ (Yeshayahu 46:6). The spice shaped like a reed carries the name too, וּקְנֵה בֹשֶׂם (Shemos 30:23).

חלק.sense: To divide, whence חֵלֶק, a portion, and חֶלְקָה, a plot of ground. A second sense is smooth, whence smooth speech and flattery.

more.t: וַיַּחְלְקוּ אֶת הָאָרֶץ (Yehoshua 14:5), they divided the land, and חִלְקוּ שְׁלַל אֹיְבֵיכֶם (Yehoshua 22:8). On וַיֵּחָלֵק עֲלֵיהֶם לַיְלָה (Bereishis 14:15) he glosses that he overtook them at midnight. The nouns are חֵלֶק, a portion, and מַחֲלֹקֶת, a division.
A holding of fields is called a חֶלְקָה, he says, because this is one portion and that another: הַחֶלְקָה אֲשֶׁר לִי (Shmuel II 14:31) and חֶלְקַת הַשָּׂדֶה (Rus 4:3).

וְאָנֹכִי אִישׁ חָלָק (Bereishis 27:11), I am a smooth man, and מִן הָהָר הֶחָלָק (Yehoshua 11:17), which he explains as the mountain that had no trees on it; Yonasan renders that one from the first sense, as a divided mountain. The river stones are named from it as well, חַלֻּקֵי אֲבָנִים מִן הַנַּחַל (Shmuel I 17:40), because they are smooth.

חָלְקוּ מַחְמָאֹת פִּיו (Tehillim 55:22), the butter of his mouth was smooth, and לְשׁוֹנָם יַחֲלִיקוּן (Tehillim 5:10). The nouns are מֵחֶלְקַת לָשׁוֹן נָכְרִיָּה (Mishlei 6:24) and דַּבְּרוּ לָנוּ חֲלָקוֹת (Yeshayahu 30:10), and with the letters doubled וַחֲלַקְלַקֹּת (Tehillim 35:6). All of them, he says, are softness and smoothness, and so of words, the softening and enticing of the tongue and its deceit.

לַחֲלִק מִשָּׁם בְּתוֹךְ הָעָם (Yirmiyahu 37:12) he takes as slipping away, which lies near the sense of smoothness: Yirmiyahu wished to slip out from there. He allows that it may belong to the first sense instead.

חמר.sense: Red wine; clay and mortar; a heap; the measure חֹמֶר, a kor; and חֲמוֹר, the donkey.

more.t: וְיַיִן חָמַר (Tehillim 75:9), and wine that is red. The Targum of יַיִן, wine, is חַמְרָא, and the verb is said of the wine itself to tell that it is very red, that being its nature; in many places wine is likened to blood, וְדַם־עֵנָב תִּשְׁתֶּה־חָמֶר (Devarim 32:14), and you drank the blood of the grape as wine. So too כֶּרֶם חֶמֶד (Yeshayahu 27:2), a vineyard of delight, named for the worth and the redness of its wine. Red in Arabic, he notes, is אחמא"ר.

more.h: Clay, and two kinds of it
more.t: וַתַּחְמְרָה בַחֵמָר (Shemos 2:3), she daubed it with clay: mortar made of lime and sand, to build with and to smear on. Some say it is a kind of pitch. In וְהַחֵמָר הָיָה לָהֶם לַחֹמֶר (Bereishis 11:3) the two stand one against the other, חֵמָר the lime mortar and חֹמֶר the earthen clay. The earthen clay is what is meant in תִּתְהַפֵּךְ כְּחֹמֶר חוֹתָם (Iyov 38:14), it turns about like the clay of a seal, and in אֲנַחְנוּ הַחֹמֶר (Yeshayahu 64:7), we are the clay; and the lime in בֶּאֱרֹת חֵמָר (Bereishis 14:10).

יֶהֱמוּ יֶחְמְרוּ מֵימָיו (Tehillim 46:4), its waters roar and are troubled, since turbid water is like clay. With the last root letters doubled, פָּנַי חֳמַרְמְרֻה, my face is troubled from weeping (Iyov 16:16), and מֵעַי חֳמַרְמָרוּ (Eichah 1:20), my innards are troubled.

וְחֹמֶר שְׂעֹרִים (Hoshea 3:2), a chomer of barley, and לָשֵׂאת מַעְשַׂר הַחֹמֶר (Yechezkel 45:11): the measure is a kor, ten ephahs, which are thirty se'ah. Apart from the measure it is a heap: חֹמֶר מַיִם רַבִּים (Chavakuk 3:14), a heap of many waters, and חֳמָרִם חֳמָרִם (Shemos 8:10), heap upon heap; in another form, חֲמוֹר חֲמֹרָתָיִם (Shoftim 15:16), a heap, two heaps.

חֲמוֹר לֶחֶם (Shmuel I 16:20) may be a heap of bread, or else may be short of a word and mean a donkey carrying bread, as חֲמֹר גָּרֶם (Bereishis 49:14), which he reads as a strong donkey with bones. On אֶחְבְּשָׁה־לִּי הַחֲמוֹר וְאֶרְכַּב עָלֶיהָ (Shmuel II 19:20), let me saddle the donkey and ride upon her, he says the feminine may be because it was a she-donkey, or because the word is said of the beast as a beast.

more.h: A donkey's head, and the yachmur
more.t: עַד הֱיוֹת רֹאשׁ־חֲמוֹר בִּשְׁמֹנִים כֶּסֶף (Melachim II 6:25) he takes plainly, a donkey's head sold for eighty of silver, as Targum Yonasan renders it רֵישָׁא דַחֲמְרָא, a donkey's head; others read the word there as the measure, as in מַעְשַׂר הַחֹמֶר (Yechezkel 45:11). Of אַיָּל וּצְבִי וְיַחְמוּר (Devarim 14:5), Rabbi Yonah wrote that Arabic calls it by that name, and that it is a beast like a large goat.

שֹכר.sense: To hire, with שָׂכִיר, a hired man, and שָׂכָר, a wage; and a second sense he takes as stopping water up, or else as making nets.

more.t: כִּי שָׂכֹר שְׂכַרְתִּיךָ (Bereishis 30:16), I have surely hired you, and בְּיוֹמוֹ תִתֵּן שְׂכָרוֹ (Devarim 24:15), on his day you shall give him his wage. The man is אִם־שָׂכִיר הוּא (Shemos 22:14), if he is a hired man; the nouns are שָׂכָר and שֶׂכֶר, a wage, and מַשְׂכֻּרְתֶּךָ, your hire. In the passive, שְׂבֵעִים בַּלֶּחֶם נִשְׂכָּרוּ (Shmuel I 2:5), those who were full of bread hired themselves out for bread.

וְשֹׂכֵר כְּסִיל וְשֹׂכֵר עֹבְרִים (Mishlei 26:10), one who hires a fool and hires those passing by, he leaves standing in three ways. Rabbi Yonah reads the great man of the people as the one who wounds everybody and rules them, paying the fool and pressing him into his service, and hiring the עֹבְרִים, the men who will not obey, after מַדּוּעַ אַתָּה עוֹבֵר אֵת מִצְוַת הַמֶּלֶךְ (Esther 3:3), why do you transgress the king's command. His brother Rabbi Moshe ties the pasuk to the one before it, חוֹחַ עָלָה בְיַד־שִׁכּוֹר (Mishlei 26:9), a thorn came up in a drunkard's hand, and reads רב there as many: the fool who rules by many proverbs, and the man who hires him for them, come to one and the same thing. Rav Saadiah Gaon takes the word not from hiring but from shutting, as כִּי יִסָּכֵר פִּי דוֹבְרֵי־שָׁקֶר (Tehillim 63:12), the mouth of those who speak falsehood shall be stopped: the fool begrudges the word of wisdom and shuts his mouth from teaching it to the fool and to the wayfarer who asks him.

גַּם־שְׂכִרֶיהָ בְקִרְבָּהּ (Yirmiyahu 46:21), her hired men in her midst: even the troops hired to fight for them were like fatted calves that cannot fight, for they too turned and fled together, a fat and pampered man being no fighter. Others read the word as her camels and her honoured men, and so the Targum renders it, אַף רַבְרְבָהָא בְגַוָהּ, even her great ones in her midst.
בְּתַעַר הַשְּׂכִירָה (Yeshayahu 7:20), with a hired razor, because the razor a man hires is the good and sharpened one. By the other reading above it is the great razor.

כָּל־עֹשֵׂי שֶׂכֶר (Yeshayahu 19:10) he has already explained under the root written with a samech, together with וַיִּסָּכְרוּ מַעְיְנֹת תְּהוֹם (Bereishis 8:2), the fountains of the deep were stopped up. He offers here besides that שֶׂכֶר may be a net, so that they are men who make nets to catch fish, and brings Chazal in Sanhedrin, where שכר is a net and בזאי is the bird the nobles fly at other birds, a falcon or its like. The Baal HaAruch explains it the same way.

שׁכר.sense: To be drunk, with שִׁכָּרוֹן, drunkenness, and שִׁכּוֹר, a drunkard; שֵׁכָר for wine and for anything else that intoxicates; and אֶשְׁכָּר, a gift.

more.t: וַיֵּשְׁתְּ מִן־הַיַּיִן וַיִּשְׁכָּר (Bereishis 9:21), he drank of the wine and became drunk. But שָׁכְרוּ וְלֹא־יַיִן (Yeshayahu 29:9) is that they are drunk and not from wine, and וּשְׁכֻרַת וְלֹא מִיָּיִן (Yeshayahu 51:21) is one drunk with troubles and not with wine. Where the verb takes an object it is to make drunk: וְהִשְׁכַּרְתִּים לְמַעַן יַעֲלֹזוּ (Yirmiyahu 51:39), I will make them drunk that they may exult, and אַשְׁכִּיר חִצַּי מִדָּם (Devarim 32:42), I will make My arrows drunk with blood.

Being drunk with wine, he says, is to drink what being sated is to food; but a man may drink until he neither feels nor understands. וְהוּא שִׁכֹּר עַד־מְאֹד (Shmuel I 25:36), he was very drunk, and וַיַּחְשְׁבֶהָ עֵלִי לְשִׁכֹּרָה (Shmuel I 1:13), Eli took her for a drunken woman.
